title: 19 Million Eggs Recalled Across Six US States Over Salmonella Risk
excerpt: Midwest Poultry Services has voluntarily recalled nearly 1.6 million dozen eggs sold at Kroger, Brookshire Grocery, and other retailers after potential Salmonella Enteritidis contamination was detected at two Texas farms.
body:
• Midwest Poultry Services has recalled 1,589,577 dozen eggs — roughly 19 million individual eggs — produced at two Texas farms between June 6 and July 3, 2026.
  • The eggs were sold at Kroger stores in Texas and Louisiana, Brookshire Grocery stores across six states, and other smaller retailers; no illnesses have been reported so far.
  • Consumers should check carton codes P-1950 or 0840962 with Julian dates between 157 and 184, and return affected eggs for a full refund.

What Happened

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on July 22 posted a recall notice from Midwest Poultry Services, L.P., an Indiana-based shell egg producer, covering 1,589,577 dozen white shell eggs and brown cage-free shell eggs. The eggs, produced at two of the company's Texas farms between June 6 and July 3, 2026, may be contaminated with Salmonella Enteritidis, a bacterium that can cause severe and sometimes fatal illness in young children, elderly people, and those with weakened immune systems.

https://x.com/thedailybeast/status/2080354758489940297

The company said it identified the contamination risk "through proactive environmental monitoring practices and root cause analysis" and has halted all fresh egg distribution from its Texas farms, according to Reuters.

Which Products Are Affected

The recall covers eggs sold under multiple brand names at major retailers. At Kroger stores in Texas and Louisiana, affected products include Kroger Large (12, 18, and 60 count), Kroger Extra Large (12 count), Kroger Medium (12 and 30 count), Kroger Jumbo (12 count), and Simple Truth Cage-Free eggs in brown medium and large varieties.

At Brookshire Grocery stores in Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, and Mississippi, affected brands include Brookshire's, Country Morning, and Sunups in various sizes. Bulk-grade eggs sold to smaller retail outlets and foodservice customers are also part of the recall.

The recalled cartons carry identifying codes P-1950 or 0840962 with a Julian date between 157 and 184, with sell-by or best-by dates ranging from July 20 to August 17, 2026.

How Retailers Are Responding

"Upon receiving notice of the recall, we immediately began reviewing our inventory and removing any potentially affected products from our stores."

— Brookshire Grocery, statement to PEOPLE

Brookshire Grocery said it has sourced replacement inventory and future shipments from alternate facilities and confirmed that all eggs currently on its shelves come from a different production facility. Kroger has not publicly commented on the recall.

Salmonella Enteritidis: The Risk

Salmonella Enteritidis is one of the most common Salmonella subtypes associated with eggs. According to the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, the bacterium can infect an egg while it is still forming inside the hen, during the laying process through the shell, or after laying by entering through the shell's pores. Symptoms of infection include fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps, typically appearing within 12 to 72 hours of consuming contaminated food.

No illnesses have been linked to the recalled eggs as of the announcement date, according to both the FDA and Midwest Poultry Services.

What Midwest Poultry Services Is Doing

"When we learned of a possible issue with egg safety, we began diverting eggs to a breaking plant where they would be pasteurized to kill any foodborne pathogens."

— Midwest Poultry Services LP

The company, which describes itself as family-owned and led, said it has launched an internal investigation and initiated testing protocols to identify potential sources of the contamination. It called the recall "a precautionary measure."

Safety Tips for Indian Kitchens

Eggs are a staple in many Indian households across the US, used in everything from egg curry and anda bhurji to baking. The FDA recommends consumers check their refrigerators for affected products immediately. Those who have purchased eggs with the recalled codes should not consume them and should return them to the store for a full refund.

As a general food safety practice, cooking eggs to an internal temperature of 160°F (71°C) kills Salmonella bacteria. Dishes that use raw or undercooked eggs carry higher risk. Consumers with questions can contact Midwest Poultry Services at 574-405-9531 (Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.) or email recallassistance@mpseggs.com.
